text.p: Continental Airlines Inc said in London on Thursday that it was objecting to the British government's proposed conditions for allowing a controversial alliance between British Airways and American Airlines to go ahead.

In particular, it said it did not believe that proposed conditions being discussed with the UK Office of Fair Trading would go far enough to allow Continental and others to mount real competition on transatlantic routes between the UK and US.
The core UK government proposal is that BA and American release a total of 168 weeekly takeoff and landing slots at London's Heathrow airport.

But Continental said in a statement released here it alone would require enough runway slots and facilties at the airport to operate at least six daily return flights between New York Newark and Heathrow, "as well as the ability to add flights in response to competitive actions by the BA/American combine".
This meant it would be asking Britain to make available 140 weekly runway slots at Heathrow, along with "ample" appropriate facilities, the airline added.

Otherwise, Continental said, the BA/American alliance would strangle competition on transatlantic routes, controlling more than 60 percent of all seats on the UK/U.S. market and more than 70 percent of seats from Heathrow to the United States.

"As a result, the OFT's proposed remedies would result in a far less competitive marketplace than air travellers enjoy today, even if one assumes an (Anglo-US) Open Skies (trade) agreement was struck," the airline's statement added.
Chairman Gordon Bethune called the alliance between BA and American effectively the world's largest airline merger.

"BA and AA promise to deliver the ultimate transportation benefit but, under a cold light and met with the full impact of ice-hard scrutiny, this huge deal is just as attractive to travellers as that last great wonder of the Altantic, The Titanic," he said.
Last month the OFT asked other airlines participating in the market to submit their comments on its proposals by January 10.

Earlier this week managers of another U.S. major, Delta Air Lines, said their general position would be that the planned constraints were not restrictive enough to allow rivals to establish "meaningful competition" at Heathrow.
The U.S. government is also likely to have a say in the final form of any regulatory deal that clears the way for the alliance.

Washington has linked approval of the competition aspects of the deal to getting a so-called "open skies" agreement with Britain which would entail giving all U.S. airlines access to Heathrow -- regarded as Europe's most popular and lucrative hub for transatlantic air traffic.
